units.translation: d. To the Aeolidae: to the descendants of Aeolus. For Cretheus and Athamas were sons of Aeolus, son of Hellen; Aeson was son of Cretheus, and Jason son of Aeson. Abas was son of Melampus, son of Amythaon, son of Cretheus, son of Aeolus.

146-49a. And indeed the Aetolian woman, mighty: reasonably he called her Aetolian, since Thestius was an Aetolian. And he has spoken from the country, as if someone calls the Syracusan Sicilian or the Roman Italian. But Ibycus (fr. 41 B. III 249) calls her Pleuronian, and Hellanicus (4 fr. 119 J.) Calydonian. Leda was the daughter of Thestius, king of Aetolia, son of Ares and Demodice; and they say her mother was Deidamia. Eumelus (fr. 6 Kink. 191) in his Corinthiaca says that her father was Glaucus, son of Sisyphus, and her mother Panteidyia,

recounting that when his horses perished, Glaucus came to Lacedaemon and there had intercourse with Panteidyia; later she married Thestius, so that Leda, though by birth Glaucus' daughter, was called Thestius' daughter. Pherecydes in the second book (3 fr. 9 J.) says that Leda and Althaea were born to Thestius from Laophonte, daughter of Pleuron. That she is Glaucus' daughter, Alcman (fr. 8 B. III 17) also hints, saying 'whom the blessed daughter of Glaucus bore'. They say that Polydeuces was son of Zeus, and Castor son of Tyndareus. 'Telygetous' here means 'beloved', but Homer uses it for those born in old age.
b. Aetolian, either because of the country or from Aetolus the hero.

152. From Arene: Pherecydes (3 fr. 127 J.) says that the mother of Idas and his brothers was Arene, after whom the city is named; Pisander (16 fr. 2 J.) says Polydora; Theocritus (XXII 206) says Laocoosa. These men were contemporaries of the Dioscuri. Arene is a city of the Peloponnese near Pylos; and Homer (B 591): 'and they dwelt in Pylos and lovely Arene'.
